pr_title: WIP: Add 20% random jitter to client-go's backoff
pr_body:
/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
This goal of this PR is to add random jitter to client-go's backoff.

The current form of this PR introduces an unconfigurable, additive 20% jitter to each backoff cycle.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #87915

**Special notes for your reviewer**:
The exact implementation and behavior is open to debate.

issue_context.title: Backoffs should have jitter
issue_context.body:
client-go implements exponential backoff. This backoff is used in the control plane, kubelets, and by many 3rd parties. There are many cases where backoff would be improved by jitter.

For example, suppose many pods enter a CrashLoopBackOff at once, due to a shared failure.
With no jitter, this (potentially large) group of pods will all retry and start at the same time, hammering the Kubernetes API and other systems. In addition, recovery would be delayed up to 5 minutes (the max backoff in that context) until all pods start at the same time.
comments: /cc @vincepri might be somewhat relevant to our interests

> #87829 just went in-- related.

Naively, why does the api machinery have a separate implementation from client-go backoff?

I support client-go tweaks for this purpose, but as time goes on we will accumulate more and more non-client-go clients. So the solution here is really to make the control plane more robust.

This has been in flight for a while: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/20190228-priority-and-fairness.md

For the specific case you mention, if the system is configured right, the clients will end up grouped in a few queues, interfering with each other but not with other api callers. Waiting in a queue rather than failing immediately (current max-in-flight limit behavior) also solves the problem of clients going into a hot loop and retrying very rapidly.

We currently expect a usable alpha in 1.18.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/87794 is the thing I actually should have linked as relevant.

As for why it's divergent, I think the client go backoff just isn't in the right shape for our collection of WaitXXX methods; also apimachinery can't import the client.

> I support client-go tweaks for this purpose, but as time goes on we will accumulate more and more non-client-go clients. So the solution here is really to make the control plane more robust.
> 
> This has been in flight for a while: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/20190228-priority-and-fairness.md
> 
> For the specific case you mention, if the system is configured right, the clients will end up grouped in a few queues, interfering with each other but not with other api callers. Waiting in a queue rather than failing immediately (current max-in-flight limit behavior) also solves the problem of clients going into a hot loop and retrying very rapidly.
> 
> We currently expect a usable alpha in 1.18.

This seems to address a subset of concerns. Mass pod startup can cause strain outside of the apiserver (EG IO-heavy bootstrapping for the app). Additionally, it doesn't look like this addresses the lock-step nature of unjittered backoffs (which still cause an artificial recovery delay, aside from the load concerns in a thundering herd). Not sure if I'm missing something here - these look like complimentary solutions to me.

> This seems to address a subset of concerns. Mass pod startup can cause strain outside of the apiserver (EG IO-heavy bootstrapping for the app). 

What is the scenario in which a client go jitter changes mass pod *start* behavior? I agree that is a potential problem (assuming I understand you) but I don't see the connection, I'd expect e.g. jittering watch deliveries as more targeted at that.

> Additionally, it doesn't look like this addresses the lock-step nature of unjittered backoffs (which still cause an artificial recovery delay, 

Maybe-- everyone will be sitting in a queue for different lengths of time, so it should help somewhat. (we could go even further and add on the time spent waiting for the network to the delay for the next round, but a jitter is probably easier.)

That's assuming that apiserver is healthy enough to put that many connections on hold; we know apiserver can do it in steady state because the vast majority of these clients are watching stuff, the question is mostly about the seconds after it (tries to) start.

> aside from the load concerns in a thundering herd). Not sure if I'm missing something here - these look like complimentary solutions to me.

Yes, they are complementary. My point is more that we, the control plane, need to get our house in order before we start scolding clients too much about their behavior :) I really think the control plane can and should improve 10x.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/87795 addresses list/watch calls, and there's still plenty of room to address all calls with your change (which I left comments on).
Maybe an item to discuss live in SIG meeting?

review_comments:
I am confused about why it constructs a `rand` per entry? Is it for locking?

If this is really necessary, I recommend having Backoff construct a `rand` and use that to generate the seeds--that is easier to reason about.

Like, I think the current code in this PR has the surprising property that perfectly synchronized clocks would cause clients failing simultaneously to fall into exactly the same random number sequence? Admittedly that's not currently super likely, but it's bad karma to leave things like that laying around.
Yeah, I can't decide why this is necessary.
This was a misunderstanding on my part about how seeds work.
The old code had this problem too, but personally I find all the casts to be far worse than the `if` statement that `integer.Int64Min` lets us avoid.
Since folks can't change it, it's not really a default, it's just the `JitterRatio`. Does it need to be public?
It was exported for the purpose of tests - I'll reevaluate if it's necessary in that context.
nit: use `rand.Uint64()`; rand should already be seeded correctly, so using it means client-go won't be opinionated about how that is done.
I'm concerned about this, rand.Uint64() is part of the global rand lock.  That's somewhat concerning and may have a more negative impact than anticipated.  Would need to be tested at scale.
I doubt that'll be an issue, but if it is, we could construct an intermediate rand instance for generating these seeds.

I greatly appreciate the test, but this is kind of a change detector right now, and it'll be awkward to update if we e.g. change the ratio (as I'm sure you must already appreciate, having somehow gotten the correct batch of random numbers in here).

I suggest instead
* make jitter a field so you can vary it; set it to 0 for these tests, so that they continue to test the exponential math exactly
* make a new test that proves that the jittered time is always in the expected bounds
* make a test that proves that jitter + exponential backoff stays within the expected bounds
